title: 3 Days on Maui: An Honest First-Timer Itinerary
intro: Three days is enough to fall for Maui and not enough to see it. The island is bigger and slower than it looks on a map, so the trick is to pick two or three things and do them well instead of chasing a checklist. This plan assumes you land midday on day one and fly out the morning of day four.

sections.h2: How to think about three days
sections.body:
Maui rewards people who stay in one region and take short trips out, not people who cross the island twice a day. Driving from Kāʻanapali on the west side to Hāna on the east is a full day by itself. Choose a home base, build each day around one anchor activity, and leave the afternoons loose.

On a short trip you have to pick. The two big single-day commitments, a Haleakalā sunrise and the Road to Hāna, both eat most of a day and cannot really be combined. Do one this trip and save the other.

Do not schedule anything hard the day you arrive. Pick up the rental car, get groceries and water, and walk onto a calm beach in the late afternoon. If you are on the west side, Kāʻanapali or Napili Bay are easy first stops. In South Maui, the Kamaʻole beaches in Kīhei work well. Check today's conditions before you get in, and watch the lifeguard flags rather than the crowd.

sections.h2: Day 2: sunrise volcano or the Hāna road
sections.body: This is your big day, and you choose one. Haleakalā sunrise means a 3 a.m. alarm, near-freezing air at the 10,000-foot summit, and a reservation you must book ahead through recreation.gov (see the sunrise reservation guide). The Road to Hāna is the other option, a slow 10-to-12-hour loop of waterfalls, one-lane bridges, and 600-plus curves. Both are worth it. Neither should be rushed.

Spend the morning in the water while it is calm, since wind and swell usually build through the day. Molokini snorkel tours leave early from Māʻalaea; shore snorkeling is good at Kapalua Bay and, in summer, Honolua Bay. Read the snorkel safety guide first, because most Maui ocean trouble happens to snorkelers who misjudge conditions. Keep the afternoon for a slow lunch and packing.

For a first trip, West Maui (Kāʻanapali, Kahana, Kapalua) or South Maui (Kīhei, Wailea) both make sense. Both put you near calm beaches, restaurants, and snorkel boats. South Maui is a bit more central for Haleakalā and the airport; West Maui is closer to whale-watching waters in winter. See what to know for a first trip for the fuller rundown.

sections.h2: What to skip on a short trip
sections.body: Do not try to do Haleakalā and Hāna on back-to-back days; you will be exhausted and driving tired on dangerous roads. Skip the far-flung stuff, like the back road past Hāna or a Lānaʻi ferry day. On West Maui, plan around Lahaina: most of historic Front Street is still a closed rebuilding zone after the 2023 fire, so treat the town with care and stick to the businesses that have reopened rather than the fire site.

keyFacts: Pick one big day-trip: Haleakalā sunrise OR the Road to Hāna, not both.
Haleakalā sunrise entry (3–7 a.m.) needs a recreation.gov reservation booked ahead, plus the $30 per-vehicle park fee.
The Road to Hāna is a 10–12 hour round trip with stops; the drive alone is about 2.5–3 hours each way.
Base in West Maui or South Maui to keep daily drives short.
Most of historic Lahaina Front Street remains closed post-fire; nearby Kāʻanapali and Kapalua are fully open.
cautions: Never judge ocean safety by how calm it looks or how many people are in the water. Check live conditions and defer to lifeguards and posted flags every time.
A Haleakalā sunrise means a pre-dawn drive down a steep mountain road afterward while tired. Bring a warm layer, and pull over if you are drowsy.
On West Maui, do not treat the Lahaina fire zone as a sightseeing stop. Much of it is a closed construction area and a place people lost their homes.

title: 5 Days on Maui: The Full-Island Itinerary
intro: Five days is the sweet spot for a first Maui trip. You can do both signature outings, spend real time in the water, and still have a day that is nothing but a beach and a book. This plan keeps daily drives reasonable and leaves margin for weather and jet lag.

sections.body: With five days you can fit the two anchor trips that a shorter visit forces you to choose between: a Haleakalā sunrise and the Road to Hāna. Space them out. Put easy beach and snorkel days between the big ones so you are not driving hard two days running. If your flights cost you the first afternoon and last morning, you still have three and a half usable days.

sections.h2: Should you split where you stay
sections.body: For five nights, most people are happier in one base than packing up midway. West Maui and South Maui both work, and each is roughly 45–75 minutes from the airport and Haleakalā. A split (say two nights near Hāna, three on the west or south side) suits people who want to slow down on the east side, but it costs you a repacking day. See first-time basics before deciding.

sections.h2: Days 1–2: settle in and get in the water
sections.body: Arrive, stock the fridge, and start slow on a calm beach like Kamaʻole III in Kīhei or Kāʻanapali on the west side. Use day two for morning snorkeling, when the water is usually flattest, at Kapalua Bay or on a Molokini boat trip. Check the conditions hub each morning and read the snorkel safety guide first.

Book a sunrise reservation ahead through recreation.gov, or skip the 3 a.m. alarm and go for sunset or midday instead, which need no timed reservation. The summit sits above 10,000 feet and can be near freezing with strong wind even in summer, so pack a real jacket. Full details are in the sunrise reservation guide. Spend the rest of the day upcountry in Kula or Makawao, then rest.

Start at dawn with a full tank, food, and downloaded maps, since cell service drops out for long stretches (see the connectivity guide). The drive is about 2.5–3 hours each way over 620 curves and 59 bridges, 46 of them one lane. Waiʻānapanapa State Park with its black-sand beach requires a separate advance reservation for out-of-state visitors. Turn around with enough daylight to get back; the road is much harder in the dark.

sections.h2: Day 5: whales, turtles, or nothing at all
sections.body: Save the last full day for something easy and weather-flexible. In winter (roughly December through April) a whale-watch boat is the standout; see the whale-watching guide. Year-round you have a good chance of seeing honu resting on the sand; the sea turtle guide explains where and the legal distance to keep. Otherwise, pick your favorite beach from the week and do nothing.

Maui's east and up-mountain areas can be rainy while the coast stays dry, and winter brings the occasional storm. Keep at least one flexible day so you can swap a wet Hāna morning for a sunny south-shore one. The month-by-month weather guide and packing list help you plan around it.

keyFacts: Five days lets you do both Haleakalā and the Road to Hāna without stacking them back-to-back.
One base usually beats splitting for five nights; West and South Maui are each about 45–75 minutes from the airport.
Haleakalā sunrise needs a recreation.gov reservation; sunset and midday do not.
Waiʻānapanapa State Park (the black-sand beach on the Hāna road) requires a separate advance reservation for non-residents.
Whale-watch boats run roughly December through April, with peak activity in January–March.
cautions: Drive the Road to Hāna during daylight only. The one-lane bridges, blind curves, and cliff edges are far more dangerous after dark or in heavy rain.
Ocean conditions change by beach, shore, and hour. Check live conditions and follow lifeguards rather than assuming a calm-looking bay is safe.
The Haleakalā summit can be near freezing with high wind year-round. People underdress for it and get genuinely cold; bring a warm layer even in July.

title: 1 Day on Maui from the Kahului Cruise Port
targetQuery: maui cruise port one day kahului
intro: Cruise ships calling at Maui now dock at Kahului Harbor, the island's working commercial port on the north shore. It is an industrial pier with nothing walkable nearby, so your day depends entirely on how you get out and how realistic your plan is. With one port day and a hard back-aboard time, less is more.

sections.h2: What the port is actually like
sections.body: Kahului is Maui's only active cruise port; Lahaina Harbor no longer takes cruise tenders after the 2023 fire. Kahului is a cargo and cruise dock, not a tourist waterfront. There are no shops, beaches, or restaurants within walking distance. To do anything you need a ship excursion, a pre-booked tour, a rental car, or a taxi. The town of Kahului, with its stores and the airport, is a short drive away but is not a scenic stop.

Your realistic options are a cruise-line shore excursion, an independent tour that picks up at the port, a taxi or rideshare, or a rental car arranged in advance. Rental counters are near the airport a few miles away, and shuttle logistics eat into a short day. Whatever you choose, pad your return time heavily; the ship will not wait, and Maui traffic through Kahului and Pāʻia can be slow.

sections.h2: A realistic radius for one day
sections.body: From Kahului, the beaches and towns of the north shore, central valley, and the near west and south sides are reachable. The far ends of the island are not. Do not attempt the full Road to Hāna on a port day; it alone runs 10–12 hours round trip and you will miss the ship. A short taste of the Hāna highway to Twin Falls or the Pāʻia area is the most a cruise day should attempt (see driving times).

sections.h2: Beach and snorkel options close by
sections.body: If you just want sand and water, the south-shore beaches near Kīhei, like Kamaʻole III, are an easy drive and often calm in the morning. Baldwin Beach near Pāʻia is close to the port. Hoʻokipa is a great place to watch surfers and, often, turtles resting on the sand, though it is a viewing beach more than a swimming one. Check live conditions and read the snorkel safety guide before getting in.

sections.h2: Can you do Haleakalā on a port day
sections.body: Sometimes, but carefully. A midday or self-guided summit visit is doable from Kahului in a few hours, and the sunrise reservation window (3–7 a.m.) does not apply to daytime entry. You still pay the $30 per-vehicle park fee, and the summit is above 10,000 feet and cold, so bring a jacket. Weigh the drive time against your all-aboard hour, and see the Haleakalā guide for specifics.

If your cruise calls between roughly December and April, a port-day whale-watch trip is one of the best uses of a few hours, since the humpbacks gather in the channel right off Maui. Book a boat that departs from Māʻalaea, which is close to Kahului, and confirm the return leaves you a wide margin. The whale-watching guide covers timing.

keyFacts: Kahului Harbor is Maui's only cruise port; Lahaina no longer accepts cruise tenders after the 2023 fire.
The port is industrial with no shops, beaches, or restaurants within walking distance.
Do not attempt the full Road to Hāna on a port day; it runs 10–12 hours round trip.
A daytime Haleakalā summit visit is possible from Kahului but tight against a back-aboard time; the $30 per-vehicle fee applies.
Hawaiʻi’s ~11% cruise-fare accommodations tax (Act 96) is currently BLOCKED by a federal injunction (Dec 31, 2025) and not being charged while the appeal proceeds.
cautions: Build in a large buffer for your all-aboard time. Kahului and Pāʻia traffic and long drives make it easy to cut a return dangerously close.
Do not overreach on distance. The far ends of Maui, including Hāna, cannot be safely done and undone within a single port day.
Ocean conditions vary by beach and by hour. Check live conditions and heed lifeguards; a north-shore beach that looks fine can have strong current and shorebreak.

title: The Best Time to Visit Maui: Season by Season
intro: Maui is a year-round destination, so the real question is what you want to trade. Winter brings whales, big north-shore surf, higher prices, and a bit more rain. Summer brings dry weather, warm water, and the biggest crowds of the year. Here is how the seasons actually shake out.

sections.body: For most first-timers, the shoulder months of April–May and September–October hit the best balance: warm dry-ish weather, thinner crowds, and lower prices than the winter and summer peaks. Come in winter if whales or big surf are the point. Come in summer if you want the calmest water and the driest coast and do not mind the crowds and rates.

This is high season, and it earns it. Humpback whales fill the channel between Maui and Lānaʻi, peaking in January through March; see the whale-watching guide. North-shore surf is at its biggest, which is a spectacle at spots like Honolua Bay and dangerous for swimming. December is Maui's rainiest month on average, with January and February close behind. Prices and crowds spike around the December holidays. Book early.

Spring is one of the smartest windows. The last whales trail off in April, rain eases as the island moves toward its dry season, and crowds thin out once spring break ends. Water and air are warm, and rates sit below the winter and summer peaks. If you want good weather without the highest prices, this is the stretch to target.

Summer is the driest, most reliably sunny time on the coast, and the ocean is often at its calmest and warmest. That makes it the easiest season for snorkeling and beach days with kids. It is also the busiest, especially July, with the highest crowds and among the highest prices. One thing to note: Central Pacific hurricane season runs June through November and peaks August through October, so keep an eye on forecasts.

Late September into November is the other quiet sweet spot. Summer's dry warmth largely holds, crowds drop sharply after Labor Day, and prices fall to some of the year's lowest before the holidays. The first whales start showing up in November. The tail of hurricane season lingers into November, but active storms hitting Maui directly are uncommon.

sections.h2: Crowds, prices, and how to choose
sections.body: Peak demand and peak prices cluster around late December through March and again in mid-summer. The cheapest, quietest stretches are typically April–May and October–early December (holidays aside). Match the season to your priority: whales and surf mean winter, calm warm water means summer, and value with good weather means the shoulders. Cross-check the month-by-month weather guide and the surf-season guide to line up your dates with the right shore.

keyFacts: Shoulder months (April–May, late September–November) tend to offer the best mix of weather, price, and low crowds.
Whale season runs roughly December through April, peaking January–March.
December is Maui's rainiest month on average; the driest stretch is May through October.
Summer has the calmest, warmest water and the biggest crowds and prices, especially July.
Central Pacific hurricane season runs June–November, peaking August–October.
cautions: Winter's big north-shore surf is beautiful and hazardous. High surf brings strong currents and shorebreak; check live conditions and follow lifeguards, and never turn your back on the ocean.
Hurricane season (June–November) rarely produces a direct hit, but passing storms can bring high surf and heavy rain. Monitor forecasts and heed any official warnings.
Seasonal averages are not guarantees. Any month can bring a wet week or a big swell, so plan flexible days rather than counting on perfect weather.

title: Maui Weather Month by Month: What to Actually Expect
intro: Maui's weather is mild all year, so the differences between months are smaller than in most places. What changes is the odds of rain, the size of the surf, and how many other people are on the beach. Here is a realistic month-by-month read, plus why the number on your phone often lies about your actual beach.

sections.body: Maui has many microclimates packed into one island. West and South Maui coasts (Lahaina, Kīhei, Wailea) are dry, averaging only about 10–15 inches of rain a year. Upcountry and the east side are far wetter, and Hāna gets on the order of 400 inches annually. A rainy forecast for Maui usually means the mountains and east side, not your south-shore beach. Check the live conditions hub for where you actually are.

These are the coolest, wettest months, though cool here still means coastal highs around the low 80s Fahrenheit. December through February see the most rain, largely on the windward and up-mountain sides, and the occasional winter Kona storm can flip the usual pattern and wet the south and west. North-shore surf is at its biggest. Whales peak now. Water temperatures dip to around the mid-70s. See the whale guide.

sections.h2: April–June: drying out and warming up
sections.body: Spring shifts the island toward its dry season. Rain tapers through April and May, and June is one of Maui's driest, sunniest months with steady trade winds. Air and water warm gradually. This stretch is comfortable and increasingly reliable, and it lands before the summer crowd peak. It is a strong window for calm-water beach days on the leeward coasts.

Summer is the driest and warmest period, with coastal highs in the mid-to-upper 80s and water near 80. The leeward beaches are reliably sunny, and south-shore surf picks up modestly while the north shore lies down. This is also the muggiest stretch when trade winds stall or Kona winds bring humidity from the south. Hurricane season is active in the background, peaking August–October, so watch forecasts.

sections.h2: October–December: the turn back to winter
sections.body: October often keeps summer's dry warmth with fewer crowds, making it a favorite month. Rain and surf build again through November and into December, which is statistically the wettest month. The first whales arrive in November, and by December the season is underway. Temperatures ease back toward the low 80s on the coast. Holiday-period crowds and rates climb sharply in late December.

sections.h2: Wind, humidity, and what to pack
sections.body: Trade winds from the northeast are the island's default and keep things comfortable; when they die and Kona winds take over, it feels hotter and stickier, and vog can settle in. Afternoons are usually windier than mornings, which is one reason to snorkel early. Pack layers for elevation and evenings, especially if you are heading up Haleakalā. The packing guide has the full list.

keyFacts: Coastal highs stay mild year-round: roughly low 80s °F in winter, mid-to-upper 80s in summer.
Leeward Maui (Lahaina, Kīhei, Wailea) averages only about 10–15 inches of rain a year; Hāna gets around 400.
December is the wettest month on average; May–October is the dry season, with June among the driest.
Ocean temperatures range from the mid-70s °F in winter to near 80 in late summer.
North-shore surf peaks in winter; south-shore surf is larger in summer.
cautions: Rain and surf vary enormously by shore. A stormy island forecast can mean a wet Hāna and a dry Wailea the same afternoon, so check conditions where you are.
Winter high surf on north- and west-facing shores brings dangerous currents and shorebreak. Read live conditions and follow lifeguards before entering the water.
Central Pacific hurricane season (June–November, peak August–October) can bring high surf and heavy rain even from a distant storm. Monitor official forecasts.

title: Maui Surf Season: When Each Shore Is Calm (and When It Is Not)
intro: Maui does not have one ocean season. It has several at once, and which shore is calm flips depending on the month. North and west facing beaches get pounded by winter swells that arrive from storms in the North Pacific. South shore beaches get their surf in summer from swells born far to the south. Knowing which coast is working on a given week is the difference between an easy snorkel and a scary one.

sections.h2: Winter: north and west shores get big
sections.body: From roughly November through March, and sometimes into April, North Pacific swells send surf to the north and west shores. Honolua Bay turns into a world-class surf break and is no place to snorkel then. Kapalua, Kaʻanapali, and the Lahaina-side beaches can go from flat to overhead within a day when a swell fills in. Surf forecasts are your friend in winter, because a beach that was glassy yesterday can have a dangerous shorebreak and strong currents today. Check Honolua Bay conditions and D.T. Fleming before you decide.

sections.h2: Summer: the south shore gets its turn
sections.body: From about April through September, Southern Hemisphere swells reach the south-facing shores. That means Kihei, Wailea, and Mākena see more surf and shorebreak in summer, while the north and west shores usually calm down. South swells are generally smaller than winter north swells, but Big Beach (Oneloa) at Mākena is known for a powerful shorebreak that snaps ankles and dislocates shoulders even on modest days. See Big Beach conditions before you get in.

sections.h2: The north shore is windy most of the year
sections.body: Hoʻokipa and the Paia stretch face both swell and the prevailing trade winds, so they tend to be choppy and current-prone across many months, not just one season. Hoʻokipa is a surf and windsurf spot with rocks and rip currents, better for watching than swimming for most visitors. Baby Beach in Paia is the calmer exception, protected by a reef, but it is a keiki spot, not an open-water swim.

Molokini crater and the Wailea and Kihei beaches are the more reliably protected snorkel zones in winter, which is why most snorkel boats run the south and west side then. Napili Bay and Kapalua Bay are semi-protected pockets on the west side that can still be worth it between swells. Relatively calm is not the same as safe. Any of these can turn with a new swell or an offshore wind, so treat each day on its own.

sections.h2: How to read a Maui day
sections.body: Look at the surf forecast for the shore you are visiting, not the island as a whole. Watch the water for a few minutes before entering and count the waves in a set. If a beach has lifeguards, ask them, since they know that specific break. When in doubt, pick a shore that is out of season for surf: south shore in winter, west or north-protected coves in summer. For the bigger picture on timing a trip, see best time to visit Maui and the month-by-month weather guide.

keyFacts: North and west shores are biggest November through March from North Pacific swells.
South shores (Kihei, Wailea, Mākena) get their surf April through September from south swells.
Honolua Bay is a winter surf break and not safe for snorkeling when north swell is running.
Big Beach at Mākena has a dangerous shorebreak that injures people even on small summer days.
The north shore (Hoʻokipa, Paia) is windy and current-prone across much of the year.
Molokini and the south/west protected beaches are the more reliable winter snorkel zones.
cautions: A calm beach can turn dangerous within a day when a new swell fills in. Check the forecast for that specific shore before every swim.
Big Beach shorebreak and Hoʻokipa currents injure and drown strong swimmers. Watch the water, and stay out if waves are breaking hard on sand or rock.
Surf forecasts describe open-ocean swell, not what a rip current is doing at your feet. Defer to lifeguards and live conditions over any seasonal rule of thumb.

title: Haleakalā Sunrise: Reservations, Timing, and What to Bring
intro: Watching the sun come up from the 10,023-foot summit of Haleakalā is one of the signature Maui mornings, and it takes real planning. You need a reservation to drive up for sunrise, the drive is long and dark, and the summit is genuinely cold. Show up unprepared and you will spend the whole time shivering instead of watching. Here is how the system works and what to pack.

sections.body: A sunrise reservation is required for any vehicle entering the Summit District between 3:00 AM and 7:00 AM. It costs $1.00 per vehicle and is booked only through Recreation.gov. Reservations are released 60 days in advance at 7:00 AM Hawaii time, and a smaller batch of tickets is released 48 hours before each date. They go fast, so set a reminder for the release. The reservation holder must be in the vehicle with a photo ID matching the name on the ticket.

sections.h2: The reservation is separate from the entrance fee
sections.body: The $1 sunrise reservation does not cover park admission. The park entrance fee is $30 per vehicle, good for three days, or you can use an America the Beautiful annual or interagency pass for entry. That pass does not cover the $1 sunrise reservation, though, so you still need to book that separately. There are no refunds if clouds roll in, which they sometimes do.

The summit is about a two-hour drive from the Kahului, Kīhei, or Lahaina-side areas, and longer if you are starting farther out. Sunrise time shifts through the year, so check the exact time for your date and aim to be parked at least 45 minutes to an hour before, both to get a spot and to let your eyes adjust. The road climbs fast with switchbacks in the dark, so drive rested. For realistic drive times around the island, see the Maui driving times guide.

sections.h2: Dress for cold, not for Hawaiʻi
sections.body: At over 10,000 feet, summit temperatures at dawn are often in the 30s or low 40s Fahrenheit, and wind makes it feel colder. People routinely arrive in shorts and a t-shirt and are miserable. Bring a warm jacket, long pants, closed shoes, a hat, and gloves if you have them. A blanket from your rental helps. Hot coffee in a thermos is worth the effort.

sections.h2: Altitude and what else to bring
sections.body: The elevation gain is rapid, and some people feel lightheaded, short of breath, or headachy at the top. The Park Service advises that people with heart or respiratory conditions, and those who have been scuba diving within 24 hours, take altitude seriously here. Bring water, snacks, a headlamp or phone light, and a full tank of gas since there is none on the mountain. Download directions ahead of time, because cell service is unreliable up top.

sections.h2: If you miss the sunrise window
sections.body: No reservation and still want the summit? You can drive up any time outside the 3:00 to 7:00 AM window without a sunrise ticket, paying only the entrance fee. Daytime views are excellent, and sunset from the summit is spectacular and needs no timed reservation. It is a solid plan B that skips the 3 AM alarm entirely.

keyFacts: Sunrise reservations are required for vehicles entering the summit between 3:00 AM and 7:00 AM.
The reservation costs $1 per vehicle and is booked only at Recreation.gov.
Tickets release 60 days out at 7:00 AM HST, with a second batch 48 hours before.
The $30 park entrance fee (or an interagency pass) is separate from the $1 reservation.
The summit sits at 10,023 feet; dawn temperatures are often in the 30s–40s Fahrenheit.
No refunds are given for cloudy weather, and the reservation holder needs matching photo ID.
cautions: Summit cold is the most common way people get caught out. Bring a warm jacket, long pants, and closed shoes even in July.
Rapid altitude gain can cause dizziness or shortness of breath. Do not drive to the summit within 24 hours of scuba diving.
The pre-dawn drive is long, dark, and winding. Only drive it well rested, with a full gas tank and downloaded directions.

title: Whale Watching on Maui: Season, Where, and How
intro: Every winter, thousands of humpback whales swim from Alaska to the warm, shallow water between Maui, Lānaʻi, Molokaʻi, and Kahoʻolawe to mate, give birth, and raise calves. Maui is one of the best places on Earth to see them, and for a stretch of the year you can spot breaches and spouts from shore without paying for anything. Here is when they come, where to look, and the rules that protect them.

sections.body: Humpbacks start arriving as early as November and some linger into April or May. The reliable window is January through March, when the most whales are here and mother-calf pairs, breaching, and pec-slapping are at their peak. If your trip falls outside those months, you may still get lucky on the shoulders, but December and early April are hit or miss. For how this fits the rest of the calendar, see the month-by-month weather guide.

You do not need a boat. The elevated pullouts along the Honoapiʻilani Highway between Māʻalaea and Lahaina, the beaches at Wailea and Kīhei, and the coast around Kāʻanapali all give good sightlines over the whale nursery in the ʻAuʻau Channel. Bring binoculars, look for the puff of a spout, then keep watching that spot. Morning tends to have calmer wind and easier water reading. Whales can appear right off Kaʻanapali and Wailea.

Boat tours run out of Māʻalaea and Lahaina Harbor and get you closer to the action, often with a naturalist and a hydrophone to hear whale song. Many operators offer a sighting guarantee during peak season, meaning a free re-ride if no whales show. Smaller rafts feel more up-close but are a rougher, wetter ride, while larger catamarans are steadier and better if anyone gets seasick. Book ahead in January and February.

Federal law requires boats, swimmers, kayakers, and paddlers to stay at least 100 yards, about 300 feet, from any humpback in Hawaiian waters. Drones and aircraft must stay 1,000 feet above them. If a whale approaches you, the rule still applies, so the operator should put engines in neutral and let it pass. These are endangered animals protected under the National Marine Sanctuary and federal law, and the distance is not a suggestion.

The spout is the whale exhaling. A breach is a full-body leap, still not fully explained by scientists. Pec slaps and tail slaps may be communication. The eerie songs, which you can sometimes hear through the hull, are sung mostly by males. Calves are born here at around 10 to 15 feet and nurse for months before the long swim back north. You are watching a nursery, so give mothers and calves extra room.

keyFacts: Humpbacks are in Maui waters roughly November through April; peak is January through March.
The ʻAuʻau Channel between Maui, Lānaʻi, and Molokaʻi is the main nursery.
You can watch for free from highway pullouts and the Kāʻanapali, Wailea, and Kīhei coasts.
Boat tours leave from Māʻalaea and Lahaina Harbor, many with peak-season sighting guarantees.
Federal law requires staying 100 yards (300 feet) from humpbacks; drones must stay 1,000 feet up.
Humpbacks are federally protected inside the Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary.
cautions: Keep 100 yards from whales in the water and by boat. If one surfaces close, hold still and let it move on rather than swimming toward it.
Winter is also big-surf season on the north and west shores. Pick safe, stable footing for shore watching and mind the waves.
Do not fly a drone near whales. Aircraft, including drones, must stay 1,000 feet above them by law.

title: Where to See Sea Turtles on Maui (Respectfully)
intro: Green sea turtles, or honu, are common in Maui's shallow water, and seeing one glide past while you snorkel is a highlight for most visitors. They are also a protected species, and the rules about keeping your distance are real laws with real fines. Here is where to find them and how to watch without causing harm.

sections.h2: The two turtles you might see
sections.body: Most turtles you will see are green sea turtles (honu), which come into shallow reef flats to feed on algae and sometimes haul out on beaches to rest. Less common is the hawksbill (honuʻea), which is far rarer and critically endangered. Both are protected. You do not need to know which is which to give it space, but the honu is the one resting on the sand at Hoʻokipa most afternoons.

sections.h2: Hoʻokipa Beach for turtles on the sand
sections.body: Hoʻokipa, just east of Paia on the north shore, is the most dependable place to see honu resting on the beach, usually in the late afternoon around 3 to 5 PM near the rock wall at the east end. Volunteers often rope off the resting turtles. Watch from behind the rope, keep your distance, and do not walk up for a photo. The water here is rough and current-prone, so this is a viewing stop, not a swim. See Hoʻokipa conditions.

Turtles feed and rest around many Maui reefs. Napili Bay, Kapalua Bay, the Kīhei and Wailea reefs, and calmer stretches of the west side are all places snorkelers regularly encounter them. If you are in the water and a turtle swims toward you, float still and let it pass rather than chasing it. Read snorkel safety before you get in, since the best turtle reefs still have currents.

sections.h2: The distance rule and the law
sections.body: NOAA and Hawaiʻi state guidance is to stay at least 10 feet, about 3 meters, from a turtle whether on land or in the water. Never touch, feed, chase, or ride one. Honu are protected under the federal Endangered Species Act and Hawaiʻi law, and harassment can bring fines reported up to $100,000. Touching a turtle can also transfer harmful bacteria and stress the animal, so hands off is for its sake as much as yours.

Use a zoom or just enjoy it with your eyes instead of pushing closer for a shot. Do not block a turtle's path to the surface, since it needs to breathe. Keep dogs away from resting turtles on the beach. If you see someone harassing a turtle, you can report it to NOAA. Reef-friendly habits help too, so use reef-safe sunscreen to protect the reefs they feed on.

keyFacts: Green sea turtles (honu) are the common species; hawksbills (honuʻea) are rare and critically endangered.
Hoʻokipa Beach near Paia is the most reliable spot for turtles resting on the sand, often 3–5 PM.
Turtles are seen in the water at Napili, Kapalua, and the Kīhei and Wailea reefs.
NOAA and state guidance: stay at least 10 feet (3 meters) away on land and in the water.
Honu are protected under the federal Endangered Species Act and Hawaiʻi law.
Touching, feeding, or chasing a turtle is illegal and can bring steep fines.
cautions: Stay at least 10 feet from turtles and never touch or feed them. Harassment is a crime with fines reported up to $100,000.
Do not block a turtle's path to the surface; it needs air. Float still and let it swim past you.
Hoʻokipa's water is rough and current-prone. Treat it as a viewing beach, not a swimming one.

title: Snorkel Safety on Maui: Where People Get in Trouble
intro: Snorkeling is the reason many people come to Maui, and it is also how visitors most often die here. Maui has led the state in snorkeling fatalities, and most of the people who drown are visitors, often on the first day or two of the trip. The water can look calm and still be dangerous. This is where people get in trouble and how to lower your odds.

sections.body: Many snorkeling deaths are not classic drownings from rough water. Researchers studying Hawaiʻi's cases point to a pattern where snorkelers, often new to it, struggle to breathe through the mask and snorkel and quietly develop fluid in the lungs, a condition called rapid onset pulmonary edema. It can happen in calm water, without a dramatic struggle, which is part of why bystanders often do not notice until it is too late. Age and heart or lung conditions raise the risk.

sections.h2: Test your gear before you go far
sections.body: Get comfortable with your mask and snorkel in shallow water where you can stand before heading over the reef. Make sure the mask seals and you can breathe easily without gulping or panicking. Ill-fitting rental gear is a common problem. If breathing feels like work, stop, stand up, and fix it. Full-face snorkel masks have been questioned in some of these cases, so many locals prefer a traditional mask and snorkel you can clear.

Black Rock at Kaʻanapali is popular and has some of the most snorkel drownings in the state, with strong currents off the north side of the point and no lifeguards. Honolua Bay is calm and stunning in summer but gets strong currents that pull you toward the exposed outer reef when surf is up, plus a slippery boulder entry. Both look inviting and both catch people out. Check Kaʻanapali and Honolua Bay conditions first, and see the dangerous beaches overview.

sections.h2: Currents and how to handle one
sections.body: Rip and channel currents are the thing that turns a nice swim into an emergency. Once you leave the sheltered part of a bay, the current can strengthen fast. If you get pulled out, do not fight straight back against it. Stay calm, keep your face out of the water enough to breathe, wave for help, and swim parallel to shore to get out of the current before heading in. Getting tired and panicked is what drowns people, not the distance itself.

sections.h2: Simple rules that keep you alive
sections.body: Never snorkel alone, and actually keep an eye on your buddy, not just near them. Pick beaches with lifeguards when you can, and ask them about that day's conditions. Go in the morning before the wind picks up. Do not snorkel right after a big meal, alcohol, or a red-eye flight when you are exhausted. If you have a heart or lung condition or you are not a confident swimmer, wear a flotation vest, which many rental shops provide. Check the shore's surf season so you pick a coast that is calm.

If waves are breaking where you want to enter, if you see whitewater or a churning brown line offshore, or if a lifeguard says no, do not go. There is no snorkel worth your life, and conditions that a local free-diver handles fine can drown a visitor. On a rough day, walk the beach, watch for turtles, and try again when the water settles.

keyFacts: Maui has led Hawaiʻi in snorkeling fatalities, and most victims are visitors.
Many deaths involve rapid onset pulmonary edema, which can occur in calm water without a visible struggle.
Black Rock at Kaʻanapali has strong currents, no lifeguards, and a high number of drownings.
Honolua Bay develops strong currents and a hazardous boulder entry when surf is up.
Currents strengthen once you leave the sheltered part of a bay; swim parallel to shore to escape one.
Test your gear in standing-depth water first, and consider a flotation vest if you are not a strong swimmer.
cautions: Calm-looking water is not safe water. Snorkelers drown on Maui in flat conditions, often on day one of a trip.
If breathing through your mask feels like effort, stop and stand up. Do not push on over deep water hoping it eases.
If a current pulls you out, do not fight it head-on. Stay calm, signal for help, and swim parallel to shore. Panic and exhaustion are what drown people.
No beach water is ever safe by default. Defer to lifeguards and live conditions, and stay out when in doubt.

title: Maui Driving Times: Between Towns and the Road to Hāna
intro: Maui looks small on a map and drives bigger than you expect. It is one big volcano and one long coastline that rarely goes in a straight line, so a short hop between two beaches can eat an hour. Here are honest drive times between the places you will actually go, plus a clear-eyed look at the Road to Hāna.

sections.body:
Kahului is the island's hub, and most people start here with a rental car. Rough drive times with normal traffic: Kīhei about 15 minutes, Pāʻia about 15, Wailea about 30, Lahaina about 40, Kāʻanapali about 45, and Kapalua closer to 50 to 55. The Haleakalā summit is a long climb from sea level, plan on about 1.5 hours from the airport and more from the coast.

Traffic on the Honoapiʻilani Highway between central and west Maui can add 15 to 30 minutes during the morning and evening rush. If you land late, do not underestimate the drive out to Kāʻanapali or Kapalua in the dark.

The two main lodging zones sit on opposite sides of the island. Kīhei or Wailea to Kāʻanapali runs roughly 45 to 60 minutes depending on traffic through the central plain and along the west side. Lahaina town to Kāʻanapali is only about 10 minutes. Wailea down to Mākena and Big Beach is another 15 or so past the resorts.

Because everything funnels through the isthmus between the two mountains, there is no shortcut. Budget for the full drive, and check cell coverage before you rely on live navigation on the quieter stretches.

The Hāna Highway runs about 64 miles from Kahului to Hāna (roughly 45 miles from Pāʻia), with roughly 620 curves and 59 bridges, 46 of them one lane. Driven straight through with no stops it is about 2.5 to 3 hours each way, but nobody does it that way, and you should not either. Plan a full day, 10 to 12 hours round trip, because the waterfalls, overlooks, and short trails are the whole point.

There is no gas between Pāʻia and Hāna town, a stretch of about 50 miles, so fill up before you leave. Leave early, around 7 a.m., to get ahead of the crowds and give yourself daylight for the drive back.

The black sand beach at Waiʻānapanapa State Park is one of the marquee stops, and non-resident visitors must reserve and prepay a timed entry online before arriving. Fees are $5 per person and $10 per vehicle, and reservations open 30 days ahead. Arrive within the first 30 minutes of your slot or you can be turned away. You can check current conditions on the Waiʻānapanapa page before you go.

The summit road climbs to about 10,000 feet, and the drive from the coast takes at least 1.5 to 2 hours because of the switchbacks and the elevation gain. For sunrise, you need a separate timed reservation on top of the park entrance fee. See the Haleakalā sunrise reservation guide for the full booking process and timing.

Going down, use low gear to save your brakes, and watch for cyclists and cattle on the upper stretches.

sections.h2: Timing tips that save your day
sections.body: Fuel up the night before any early start. Give the Road to Hāna and Haleakalā their own full days rather than stacking them. If you are staying in Kīhei or Wailea and want to see the west side, go early or late to dodge the highway backup. And do not plan a tight dinner reservation on the same evening you are driving back from Hāna, the return always runs longer than you think.

keyFacts: From OGG: Kīhei ~15 min, Wailea ~30, Lahaina ~40, Kāʻanapali ~45, Haleakalā summit ~1.5 hr.
Honoapiʻilani Highway traffic can add 15 to 30 minutes during rush hours.
Pāʻia to Hāna is about 64 miles, 620 curves, and 59 bridges, 46 of them one lane, 2.5 to 3 hours each way without stops.
No gas stations between Pāʻia and Hāna, roughly 50 miles, so fill up first.
Waiʻānapanapa State Park requires a prepaid timed reservation for non-residents ($5/person, $10/vehicle).
Haleakalā sunrise needs a separate reservation on top of the $30 park entrance fee.
cautions: The Road to Hāna is tiring to drive. Yield at one-lane bridges, pull over to let locals pass, and swap drivers if you can. Do not attempt the return in the dark if you are worn out.
The back side of Hāna (the Piʻilani Highway through Kaupō) is rough, remote, and has essentially no cell service. Many rental agreements discourage it, so check yours and check conditions first.
Cell coverage drops out along much of the Hāna Highway and near the Haleakalā summit. Download offline maps and do not count on live navigation.

title: Cell Service and Connectivity on Maui: Where You Will and Will Not Have Signal
intro: In the towns and resort areas, Maui's cell service handles maps, calls, and streaming without much trouble. But this is a big island with a 10,000-foot volcano, a rainforest coast, and long rural roads, and signal disappears in a lot of the places you will most want to explore. Knowing the dead zones ahead of time keeps a planning hiccup from turning into a real problem.

sections.body:
You will generally have solid coverage in and around Kahului, Kīhei, Wailea, Lahaina, Kāʻanapali, Kapalua, Pāʻia, and along the main highways connecting them. That covers most hotels, restaurants, and the drives between them. All three major carriers work on the island, and in the populated areas the difference between them is small.

Reports vary on who is best. T-Mobile is often cited as having strong combined 4G and 5G reach across Maui, while Verizon holds LTE across most of the island. Any single ranking is a guide, not a guarantee, so test your own phone once you land.

Expect little or no signal in the places that feel remote, because they are. The Hāna Highway runs spotty to dead once you are past Pāʻia. The back side of Haleakalā, the Piʻilani Highway from Kīpahulu through Kaupō, has essentially no native coverage from any carrier. The Haleakalā summit and crater area is patchy and carrier-dependent. ʻĀhihi-Kīnaʻu and the upper West Maui mountains are also unreliable. Plan as if you will have no signal at any trailhead or remote beach.

The state has talked about adding coverage along the Hāna Highway, but do not plan around promised towers. Treat the whole east side as offline. See the Road to Hāna driving guide for how that affects a day out there.

Download an offline map of the island before you go, Google Maps lets you save an offline area. Screenshot directions, reservation confirmations, and any addresses you will need, including your Haleakalā sunrise reservation and your Waiʻānapanapa slot. Tell someone your plan and expected return time if you are hiking, since you may not be reachable on the trail.

For a Hāna or Haleakalā outing, treat your phone as a camera, not a lifeline. A cheap paper map is a fair backup if you rely on data to get around.

Most hotels, vacation rentals, cafes, and many restaurants have Wi-Fi, so you can catch up on messages and check beach conditions when you are back in town. If you work remotely or need dependable connectivity, base yourself in a hub like Kīhei, Wailea, or the Kāʻanapali–Kapalua corridor and do not count on signal during day trips east or up the volcano.

keyFacts: Good coverage in Kahului, Kīhei, Wailea, Lahaina, Kāʻanapali, Kapalua, Pāʻia, and along the main highways.
Little or no signal along much of the Hāna Highway past Pāʻia and near the Haleakalā summit.
The back-side Piʻilani Highway (Kīpahulu to Kaupō) has essentially no coverage from any carrier.
All three major carriers work in populated areas; T-Mobile and Verizon are both widely used on Maui.
Download offline maps and screenshot reservations before heading east or up the volcano.

internalLinks.label: Maui driving times and the Road to Hāna

cautions: Do not depend on your phone for emergencies on remote trails, the Hāna Highway, or the back side of Haleakalā. Signal can be absent for the whole outing.
Save offline maps and tell someone your plan before driving to Hāna, Kaupō, or up to the Haleakalā summit.
Coverage varies by carrier and changes over time. Treat any single dead-zone report as a guide, not a promise.

title: First Time on Maui: What to Know Before You Land
targetQuery: first time on maui what to know
intro: Maui rewards a little planning more than most places. A few of the best experiences now need reservations booked weeks out, the ocean is less forgiving than it looks, and one part of the island is still rebuilding after the 2023 fire. Here is what a first-timer actually needs to know before the plane doors open.

sections.h2: You will need a rental car, and reservations
sections.body: Maui has almost no useful public transit for visitors, so plan on a rental car and book it early. Beyond the car, two of the signature outings need timed reservations: Haleakalā sunrise (a $1-per-vehicle reservation on top of the $30 park entrance fee) and Waiʻānapanapa State Park on the Road to Hāna ($5 per person plus $10 per vehicle, prepaid). Both open a set number of days ahead and sell out. See the sunrise reservation guide for the exact timing.

sections.h2: Respect Lahaina, it is still rebuilding
sections.body: The August 2023 wildfire destroyed much of Lahaina town, and in 2026 the historic Front Street area remains largely closed to through traffic while infrastructure and storefronts are rebuilt. This is a community in recovery, not a sightseeing stop. Do not drive in to look at burn areas or photograph damaged sites. The Kāʻanapali and Kapalua resort areas nearby are fully open and welcoming visitors, and a growing number of Lahaina-area restaurants have reopened.

Maui's water can look calm and turn dangerous fast, with strong currents, shore break, and big surf that shifts by season and shore. No beach is ever simply safe. Check lifeguards and live conditions every time, and read the most dangerous beaches rundown before you pick a spot. Our snorkel safety guide covers where people most often get into trouble.

sections.h2: Distances are longer than they look
sections.body: The island is bigger than the map suggests, and the roads wind. Getting from Kīhei to Kāʻanapali can take an hour, and the Road to Hāna is a full-day commitment, not a morning drive. Cell service drops out on the east side and up the volcano, so download offline maps. The driving times guide lays out realistic estimates.

Hawaiʻi bans the sale of sunscreens with oxybenzone and octinoxate statewide, and Maui County goes further, allowing only mineral (non-nano zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) sunscreens. Bring reef-safe mineral sunscreen from home or buy it locally. The reef-safe sunscreen guide explains exactly what is allowed.

sections.h2: Pack for more than the beach
sections.body: The Haleakalā summit can sit near freezing at sunrise while the coast is warm, and the Hāna side is often wet. Bring a warm layer and a rain shell, plus water shoes for rocky entries. The packing guide covers the cold parts people forget.

keyFacts: You will need a rental car; book it early, along with any Haleakalā sunrise and Waiʻānapanapa reservations.
Haleakalā entrance is $30 per vehicle for 3 days, plus a $1 sunrise reservation; Waiʻānapanapa is $5/person and $10/vehicle.
Much of Lahaina town remains closed and rebuilding after the 2023 fire; do not visit burn areas.
Maui County allows only mineral sunscreen; chemical sunscreens with oxybenzone or octinoxate are banned statewide.
Cell service is unreliable on the Road to Hāna and near the Haleakalā summit; download offline maps.
The Haleakalā summit can be near freezing at sunrise while the coast stays warm.
cautions: No Maui beach is safe by default. Currents, shore break, and surf change with the season and the day, so check lifeguards and live conditions before every swim or snorkel.
Lahaina is a fire-recovery community, not an attraction. Stay out of closed and burn areas and give residents privacy.
The Haleakalā summit sits at 10,000 feet. Altitude, cold, and dark predawn driving catch first-timers off guard, so prepare for all three.

title: What to Pack for Maui (Including the Cold Parts)
intro: Most Maui packing lists stop at swimsuits and flip-flops, and then people freeze at the Haleakalā summit and get soaked on the Hāna side. The coast is warm year-round, but the island has a 10,000-foot volcano and a rainforest, and you will want gear for both. Here is what actually earns space in the bag.

sections.h2: The cold you did not expect
sections.body: The Haleakalā summit sits around 10,000 feet, and at sunrise it can hover near freezing while Kīhei is still warm and dark below. If sunrise on the volcano is on your list, pack a warm jacket, long pants, a hat, and gloves. This is the single most common packing miss on Maui. Check the sunrise reservation guide so you book the slot and dress for the summit, not the beach.

sections.h2: Rain gear for the east side
sections.body: The Road to Hāna and the windward, rainforest side of the island are wet a lot of the year, and passing showers are normal even on sunny days. A light rain shell packs down small and keeps a waterfall stop from ending your day. Quick-dry clothes beat cotton once you are hiking muddy trails. See the Road to Hāna guide for how wet a full day out there can get.

Maui County allows only mineral sunscreen (non-nano zinc oxide or titanium dioxide), and chemical formulas with oxybenzone and octinoxate are banned for sale statewide. Bring mineral sunscreen from home or buy it locally, and pack a rash guard or sun shirt to cut how much you need. The reef-safe sunscreen guide spells out what is allowed.

Many Maui entries are rocky or have sharp reef, so water shoes or reef booties save your feet. Bring your own snorkel and mask if you have them, since rentals get old and leaky. A dry bag keeps your phone and keys safe at the beach. Before you pick a spot, read the snorkel safety guide and check live conditions.

Pack sandals for town and the beach, plus one pair of closed-toe shoes with grip for trails and lava rock. A small daypack carries water, snacks, and layers for Haleakalā or a Hāna stop. Reusable water bottles matter, hydration is easy to neglect in the heat and at altitude.

Bring a portable phone battery, since cell coverage drops on the east side and you will use your phone as a camera. Download offline maps before you go, see the connectivity guide. Motion-sickness remedies help on the winding Hāna Highway. A hat, polarized sunglasses, and after-sun lotion round out the kit.

keyFacts: Pack a warm jacket, long pants, hat, and gloves for Haleakalā sunrise, which can be near freezing at 10,000 feet.
Bring a light rain shell and quick-dry clothes for the wet east side and the Road to Hāna.
Only mineral sunscreen is allowed in Maui County; bring reef-safe mineral formulas plus a rash guard.
Water shoes protect your feet on rocky and reef entries.
A portable battery and offline maps cover the cell dead zones on the east side and the summit.
cautions: Cold and altitude at the Haleakalā summit are real. Underdressing for a predawn sunrise at 10,000 feet leaves people genuinely miserable and can be a health risk for some.
Water shoes help, but rocky and reef entries are still hazardous in surf. Footwear does not make an unsafe ocean safe, so check lifeguards and conditions first.
Do not bring or use chemical sunscreens with oxybenzone or octinoxate; they are banned for sale statewide and non-mineral sunscreen is restricted in Maui County.

title: Reef-Safe Sunscreen on Maui: What Act 104 Means for Your Bag
intro: You may have heard Maui has a sunscreen law and packed accordingly. The reality is two overlapping rules, and the local one is stricter than the statewide Act 104 most people know about. Getting it right is simple once you know what to look for on the label.

sections.h2: Two laws, and the stricter one wins
sections.body: Hawaiʻi's Act 104, passed in 2018 and in effect since January 1, 2021, bans the sale and distribution of sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate statewide without a prescription. That is the law people usually mean by "reef-safe." But Maui County went further with Ordinance 5306, in effect since October 1, 2022, which allows only mineral sunscreens made with non-nano zinc oxide or titanium dioxide. On Maui, the county rule is what governs your bag.

On Maui, the safe move is a mineral sunscreen whose only active ingredients are non-nano zinc oxide or titanium dioxide. Chemical sunscreens, including those with oxybenzone, octinoxate, avobenzone, octocrylene, and similar filters, are the ones to leave home. If a bottle lists a chemical UV filter as an active ingredient, it does not meet the Maui standard.

The ban covers sale, distribution, and use of non-mineral sunscreen without a prescription, so this is not only about what stores stock, it is about what you rub on before you get in the water near a reef.

Flip the bottle to the active ingredients panel. You want zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or both, and ideally the label will say non-nano. Marketing terms like "reef-friendly" or "reef-safe" are not regulated and do not guarantee compliance, so ignore the front of the bottle and read the back. When in doubt, mineral-only is the rule to remember.

Local shops, pharmacies, and grocery stores on Maui stock compliant mineral sunscreen, so you do not have to bring it if you would rather buy on arrival. If you already have a favorite mineral brand at home, pack it. Bringing a non-compliant chemical sunscreen is not worth the trouble, and you will just want the mineral kind here anyway.

The most reef-friendly approach is to wear less sunscreen and cover up more. A rash guard or sun shirt, a hat, and shade do most of the work, and you reserve mineral sunscreen for the parts you cannot cover. That is easier on the reef and on you. Our packing guide covers sun shirts and water gear.

Oxybenzone and octinoxate have been linked to coral damage, including bleaching and harm to developing coral, and elevated levels have been measured at popular Maui reefs like Honolua Bay. If you are snorkeling to see coral and sea turtles, the sunscreen on your skin is part of what keeps those reefs alive. Check live conditions before you get in, and read the snorkel safety guide first.

keyFacts: Hawaiʻi's Act 104 (effective January 2021) bans the sale of sunscreens with oxybenzone and octinoxate statewide.
Maui County Ordinance 5306 (effective October 2022) goes further, allowing only mineral (non-nano zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) sunscreens.
On Maui, mineral-only is the standard for your bag; chemical UV filters do not comply.
Terms like "reef-safe" are unregulated, so read the active-ingredient panel, not the front label.
Compliant mineral sunscreen is sold in local shops, so you can buy it on arrival.
cautions: A prescription exemption exists for medically necessary non-mineral sunscreen, but for general beach use, mineral-only is the rule on Maui.
Sunscreen choice does not change ocean risk. Reef and rocky entries, currents, and surf are still hazards, so check lifeguards and live conditions before you get in.
Non-nano mineral sunscreen is preferred; nano particles are excluded under the Maui County rule, so look for non-nano on the label.

title: Maui Travel Guide: Everything for a First Trip
intro: Maui rewards a little planning more than most places. The island is bigger than it looks on a map, the weather swings hard between the sunny leeward coast and the wet windward side, and the ocean is the single thing most first-timers underestimate. This guide walks you through when to come, how to get around, what to do, and the ocean facts that matter before you get in the water.

sections.body:
Maui is a year-round destination, but the seasons feel different. April, May, September, and October tend to bring good weather, thinner crowds, and better prices. Winter (mid-December through March) is peak season: it is the wettest time on the windward side, the busiest for whale watching, and the period when north- and west-facing shores get the largest surf. Summer is dry, hot, and crowded with families.

Whale season runs roughly December through April, with January to March the peak for humpbacks off the leeward coast. If you want the biggest surf on the north shore, come in winter; if you want the calmest water for snorkeling, summer is generally your friend. For a month-by-month breakdown, see our detailed pages below.

Best time to visit Maui and Maui weather month by month go deeper on the tradeoffs.

You will want a rental car. Public transit is limited, and the things people come to Maui for, sunrise at Haleakalā, the Road to Hāna, the beaches strung along the west and south coasts, are spread far apart. Book the car early, especially for winter and summer trips, because supply is tight and prices spike.

Driving times are longer than the mileage suggests. Kahului airport to Lāhainā or Kāʻanapali is about 45 minutes to an hour. The Road to Hāna is a full day, not a quick drive. Haleakalā summit for sunrise means leaving your hotel around 3 a.m. and requires a reservation. Plan your days around one region at a time rather than crisscrossing the island.

See Maui driving times and the Road to Hāna and Haleakalā sunrise reservations.

This is the part first-timers skip and shouldn't. The ocean is the leading cause of visitor injury and death on Maui, and most incidents happen to people who did not realize conditions had changed or picked the wrong beach for their ability. Waves that look small from the sand can knock you down; currents that are invisible from shore can pull you out.

A few rules that matter everywhere: never turn your back on the ocean, don't swim at a beach with no one else in the water, ask a lifeguard before you get in, and if there is no lifeguard, be far more conservative. Shore break on south and west beaches can slam swimmers into the sand. Winter surf on the north and west shores is for experienced people only.

We publish live conditions for named beaches so you can check before you go. Start with where people get in trouble snorkeling, then check today's conditions on the Maui beaches guide.

The headline experiences are snorkeling, beach days, the Road to Hāna, Haleakalā, and whale watching in season. Snorkeling is best in the morning before the wind picks up, at protected spots on the leeward coast. The Road to Hāna is about the journey, the waterfalls, black-sand beach, and rainforest, not a destination at the end. Haleakalā offers both a sunrise crater experience up top and hiking; the summit is cold and thin-aired even when the coast is warm.

If you want to see turtles, there are reliable spots where they rest and feed; keep your distance, as they are protected. Book whale-watch tours and any Haleakalā sunrise slots well ahead.

More detail: whale watching, seeing sea turtles, and our full things to do on Maui list.

Match your plan to your time. A single day, common for cruise-ship passengers docking at the port, means picking one region and one or two activities, not the whole island. Three days is enough for a beach-and-snorkel base plus one big adventure day (Hāna or Haleakalā). Five days lets you do both major drives, several beaches, and still have a rest day.

Our day-by-day plans: 1 day on Maui (cruise port), 3 days on Maui, and 5 days on Maui.

sections.h2: Practical things to pack and know
sections.body:
Bring reef-safe sunscreen. Maui law (Act 104) restricts sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate, so buy mineral-based (zinc oxide) sunscreen before or after you arrive. Pack a light rain layer and something warm for Haleakalā, water shoes if you have sensitive feet, and reef-safe options if you plan to snorkel a lot.

Cell service is good in the towns and resort areas and drops out on the Road to Hāna, in Haleakalā, and along remote coastline, so download offline maps and screenshot your reservations. Respect closures and signage; some sites require reservations or have limited parking.

See what to pack for Maui, reef-safe sunscreen and Act 104, cell service and connectivity, and first time on Maui.

keyFacts: You need a rental car; transit is limited and sights are far apart. Book early.
The ocean is the top cause of visitor injury; check conditions and pick beaches for your ability.
Whale season runs roughly December to April, peaking January to March.
Haleakalā sunrise requires an advance reservation and a roughly 3 a.m. departure.
Reef-safe (mineral) sunscreen is required under Maui's Act 104.
Spring and fall bring good weather, fewer crowds, and lower prices than winter and summer.

internalLinks.label: Driving times and Road to Hāna

cautions: Do not enter the ocean without checking current conditions; waves and currents change fast and can be dangerous even at popular beaches. We never call any beach safe.
Never swim at a beach where no one else is in the water, and ask a lifeguard before getting in.
Winter surf on north- and west-facing shores is for experienced ocean-goers only.
Cell service disappears on the Road to Hāna, in Haleakalā, and on remote coast; download offline maps and tell someone your plan.

title: Things to Do on Maui: The Honest Local List
intro: Maui's activities are spread across very different regions, from the resort-lined west and south coasts to the rainforest of the east and the volcano in the middle. This is an honest, region-by-region list of what is worth your time, plus what to do when it rains and how to have a good day without spending much. We flag the ocean risks where they matter, because a lot of the best things here happen in or near the water.

sections.body:
The west side is the classic resort coast: long sandy beaches, sunset views, and the calmest snorkeling in the mornings. Kāʻanapali Beach and its Black Rock point are the busy, easy-access option. Kapalua Bay and Nāpili Bay are more protected and good for beginners on calm days. Honolua Bay, a marine reserve to the north, has some of the best snorkeling on the island in summer, but in winter it becomes a serious surf spot and is not for swimming.

Lāhainā town was heavily affected by the 2023 wildfire; check current status and respect closures and the community before planning around it. Check conditions before snorkeling any of these on the beaches guide, and read when each shore is calm.

The south shore is dry, sunny, and lined with beaches. The Kamaʻole beaches (I and III) in Kīhei are easy family beaches with lifeguards. Wailea's beaches are calmer and front the resorts. Big Beach (Mākena) is stunning and popular, but it has a powerful shore break that regularly injures people, this is not a casual swimming beach, and its neighbor Little Beach has strong currents.

Morning snorkeling here is good before the afternoon wind. Molokini crater, a snorkel-tour destination, launches from this side. See south-shore live conditions on the beaches guide and read snorkel safety.

sections.h2: The Road to Hāna and East Maui
sections.body:
The Road to Hāna is a full-day drive along a winding, one-lane-bridge coastline through rainforest, past waterfalls, and to black-sand Waiʻānapanapa and the red-tinged Hāna area. The point is the journey. Go early, fill the gas tank, pack food, and don't rush the narrow curves. Many roadside stops have slippery rocks and flash-flood risk in the streams, so stay out of pools when rain is upstream.

Hāmoa and Hāna Bay are the main beaches out this way. Cell service is patchy to nonexistent, so download maps first. See driving times and cell service.

Haleakalā's summit sits over 10,000 feet up and feels like another planet: cold, thin air, and a crater you can hike into. Sunrise is the famous experience and requires an advance reservation; sunset and daytime visits do not. Bring real warm layers, it can be near freezing while the coast is in the 80s. Upcountry towns like Makawao and Kula offer farms, lavender, and cooler air, a good change of pace from the beach.

Plan sunrise ahead via Haleakalā sunrise reservations.

sections.h2: On the water: whales, turtles, and surf
sections.body:
In winter, whale watching off the leeward coast is reliable and memorable; boats launch from Lāhainā and Māʻalaea. Turtles rest and feed at several spots, including Hoʻokipa on the north shore, where they haul out on the sand; stay back, they are protected by law. Hoʻokipa is also a premier windsurf and surf spot, better for watching than swimming.

See whale watching and seeing sea turtles.

Rain usually means the windward and east sides; the leeward coast often stays dry, so a rainy morning is sometimes just a reason to drive to the other side of the island. When it's wet everywhere, good indoor options include the Maui Ocean Center aquarium in Māʻalaea, the Lāhainā and Kīhei shops and galleries, a farm or distillery tour Upcountry, or a spa afternoon. Rain also raises flash-flood risk in streams and waterfalls, so skip the Hāna pools and hiking near rivers on wet days.

A lot of the best of Maui costs nothing. Watch the sunset from any west-side beach, walk the Kāʻanapali beach path, snorkel from shore with your own gear at a calm morning spot, watch surfers and turtles at Hoʻokipa, stroll the Kīhei coastal boardwalk, or drive Upcountry for the views. The beaches themselves are free and public; you only pay for parking in a few spots. Just check conditions first and pick a beach that matches your ability.

keyFacts: Activities cluster by region; plan one coast or the volcano per day rather than crossing the island.
Morning is best for snorkeling before afternoon wind; leeward coast is calmest.
Big Beach (Mākena) and other south/west shores have dangerous shore break; they are not casual swim beaches.
Haleakalā sunrise needs a reservation; daytime and sunset do not.
Whale season is roughly December to April; turtles are common year-round at spots like Hoʻokipa.
The leeward (west/south) coast often stays dry when the east and windward sides are rainy.
cautions: Big Beach (Mākena) shore break regularly injures people; do not treat it as a casual swimming beach, and never dive under or turn your back on the waves. We never call any beach safe.
On the Road to Hāna and in East Maui, stay out of stream pools and waterfalls when rain is upstream; flash floods kill.
Honolua Bay and Hoʻokipa turn into serious surf spots in winter and are for experienced ocean-goers only then.
Keep well back from sea turtles and monk seals; approaching or touching them is illegal.

title: Maui Beaches: A Guide to Every Shore (with Live Conditions)
intro: Maui's beaches vary enormously by coast: the west and south are the calm, sandy, resort-lined swimming and snorkeling beaches; the north shore is windier and surf-driven; the east is remote rainforest coastline. This guide describes the character of each shore and which beaches suit families, snorkelers, surfers, or people who just want a quiet sit. Every named beach links to its live conditions page, check it before you go, because conditions change daily and we never call any beach safe.

sections.body:
The west coast is the postcard resort strip: long stretches of sand, reliable sunsets, and the island's calmest morning snorkeling. It is the best all-around area for families and beginner snorkelers on calm days, though the same north-facing points get big and dangerous in winter surf.

  • Kāʻanapali — long, busy resort beach with a snorkeling point at Black Rock; easy access, good for families.
  • Kapalua Bay — protected crescent, one of the more sheltered swim-and-snorkel spots for beginners.
  • Nāpili Bay — sandy bay good for families; watch for shore break when surf is up.
  • D.T. Fleming — pretty, less crowded, but it has strong shore break and rip currents and a history of rescues; a lifeguarded beach to respect, not underestimate.

The south shore is dry and sunny with a long line of accessible beaches, from easy family sand in Kīhei to calmer resort fronts in Wailea to the dramatic and hazardous Mākena.

  • Kamaʻole I — lifeguarded Kīhei family beach with sand and easy entry.
  • Kamaʻole III — popular family beach with a park, lifeguards, and grass; can have shore break.
  • Wailea Beach — calmer resort-front beach, good for an easy swim on gentle days.
  • Big Beach (Mākena) — spectacular wide sand, but a powerful shore break that regularly injures people; this is not a casual swimming beach.

The north shore is windier, cooler in feel, and defined by surf and windsurfing rather than easy swimming. It is a great place to watch the ocean and see turtles, and a poor place to swim casually, especially in winter.

  • Baldwin Beach — long sandy Pāʻia beach with a lifeguard; a sheltered cove ("Baby Beach") end is calmer, but the main beach has shore break and currents.
  • Baby Beach (Pāʻia) — shallow reef-protected pool popular with families on calm days; still check conditions.
  • Hoʻokipa — world-class windsurf and surf spot where turtles haul out on the sand; better for watching than swimming.

Past Kapalua, the coast turns rockier and more exposed. Honolua Bay is the standout: a marine reserve with some of Maui's best summer snorkeling, and one of its best winter surf breaks, which means it flips from calm to serious depending on the season.

  • Honolua Bay — protected snorkeling in summer over rich reef; in winter it is a premier surf spot with strong water movement and not for swimming. Rocky entry, no sand beach.

See when each shore is calm before planning a Honolua day.

The Hāna side is remote, rainy, and dramatic, reached by the long Road to Hāna. The beaches here are about scenery and character, not easy swimming, and services and cell signal are scarce.

  • Waiʻānapanapa — famous black-sand beach in a state park (reservation required to enter); powerful surf and rocky water, more for looking than swimming.
  • Hāna Bay — one of the more protected bays out east, a calmer option on gentle days.
  • Hāmoa — scenic pocket beach with sand; can have strong shore break and currents.

Plan the drive with driving times and the Road to Hāna.

sections.h2: How to choose and check before you go
sections.body:
Match the beach to the people and the day. For young kids and nervous swimmers, favor lifeguarded, protected spots like Kapalua Bay, Kamaʻole I, or Baby Beach on calm days. For snorkeling, go in the morning to leeward beaches. For surf and scenery without swimming, the north shore and Honolua are the show. Wherever you go, pick a lifeguarded beach when you can, and never swim where you're the only one in the water.

Conditions change daily and by the hour. Check the live page for any beach here before you drive out, and see where people get in trouble. Start from Maui live conditions.

keyFacts: West and south shores are calmest for swimming and snorkeling; north shore is surf and wind; east is remote.
Big Beach (Mākena), D.T. Fleming, and Hāmoa have strong shore break and currents despite looking inviting.
Honolua Bay is prime snorkeling in summer and a serious surf break in winter.
Waiʻānapanapa State Park requires an advance reservation to enter.
Morning is best for snorkeling before the wind picks up.
Each named beach has a live conditions page; check it the day you plan to go.

internalLinks.label: Where people get in trouble snorkeling

cautions: Conditions change daily; a beach that is calm one morning can have dangerous surf and currents the next. Always check the live page and never treat any beach as safe.
Big Beach (Mākena) and D.T. Fleming have powerful shore break that regularly causes serious injury; do not dive under or turn your back on the waves.
Honolua Bay and the north shore become hazardous surf spots in winter; snorkel Honolua only in calm summer conditions.
Never swim at a beach with no one else in the water, and prefer lifeguarded beaches; if there is no lifeguard, be far more conservative.
